title: METR Update: Frontier AI Fails at Designing Evaluations
summary: METR's Time Horizon 1.1 expands to 228 tasks, finding frontier models excel at coding but fail judgment work. No AI-designed evaluation deemed useful.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- METR's Time Horizon 1.1 adds 58 judgment-heavy tasks to its benchmark, including asking models to design new AI evaluations.
- Frontier models show exponential growth on coding tasks but fail open-ended judgment work, with zero useful AI evaluations produced.
- Opus 5.5 reached 'borderline above the bar' on evaluation design, up from 'clearly below' a year ago but still not research-ready.


METR released Time Horizon 1.1 on November 20, 2026, expanding its AI capability benchmark from 170 to 228 tasks and introducing judgment-heavy work for the first time. The update confirms a stark pattern:[frontier models](https://emergent.sh/glossary/frontier-model) continue exponential gains on well-defined coding and math problems but fail dramatically when asked to perform open-ended judgment work, including designing AI evaluations researchers could actually use.


## Benchmark Expansion Adds Judgment Tasks


The Time Horizon 1.1 suite introduces 58 new tasks measuring capabilities METR considers critical for autonomous AI research. Two stand out: a task asking models to design new AI evaluations METR could deploy, and a task scoring philosophical arguments. These judgment-laden exercises represent the kind of work that separates code execution from research taste, the ability to identify promising questions and frame useful experiments.


METR's Matt Putz told MIT Technology Review that judgment tasks are inherently harder to study and quantify than verifiable tasks. Computer scientist Sayash Kapoor framed the stakes more directly, arguing that research taste could become a major bottleneck on the path to automated AI research.


## Coding Performance Doubles Every Seven Months


On the well-defined side of the benchmark, the exponential trend holds. Software engineering time horizons have doubled roughly every seven months since 2021, confirming the pattern METR first documented. Models handle bounded coding and math tasks with increasing competence, pushing the envelope on work where success criteria are clear and verification is automatic.


This performance gap between verifiable and judgment tasks mirrors broader industry patterns. Frontier agents excel at constrained problems but struggle when task definitions blur or success requires human-like intuition.


## No Model Produces Useful AI Evaluation


Not one model produced an AI evaluation METR employees deemed useful for actual research. Opus 5.5, among the newest systems tested, reached what METR describes as borderline above the bar on the evaluation design task. That classification means the output shows promise but remains too flawed for METR to deploy in its own work.


The organization notes Opus 5.5 represents progress from a year ago, when models scored clearly below the bar. On the philosophical argument scoring task, models landed below human performance, though METR staff themselves disagree on how relevant that particular test is to automating AI research.


## Release Date and Reliability Caveats


Officially released on November 20, 2026, Time Horizon 1.1 arrives during a week of coverage highlighting the same frontier model pattern: strong on bounded tasks, brittle on open-ended ones. METR itself cautions that results above 16-hour time horizons remain unreliable, a reminder that the benchmark's most dramatic extrapolations sit inside error bars rather than representing confirmed capability.


The organization continues to refine its methodology for measuring judgment work, acknowledging that quantifying research taste and open-ended reasoning remains an unsolved challenge in AI evaluation.


## What This Means


METR's update underscores a capability ceiling that matters for AI safety and automation timelines. Frontier models handle structured tasks at accelerating speed but lack the judgment to design their own tests or evaluate nuanced arguments. That gap suggests automated AI research remains further out than coding-task performance alone would indicate, and reinforces the difficulty of building systems that can steer their own development. For organizations relying on AI evaluations to guide deployment decisions, the message is clear: human judgment still anchors the loop.
